subject: Business
source: Edexcel GCSE Business (1BS0) specification, Theme 1: Investigating small business (1.1 Enterprise and entrepreneurship, 1.2 Spotting a business opportunity, start of 1.3 Putting a business idea into practice). The school Drive holds only an AQA 8132 scheme of work and legacy topic folders, used for activity ideas only; all content written to the Edexcel specification and subject knowledge. Business examples are fictional unless stated | Edexcel 4BS1 specification (headline content for units 1.1-1.4, 4.1-4.3, 2.1-2.2). The older UK GCSE 1BS0 lessons in content/lessons/business/y10.json were checked: they cover aims, market research, segmentation and revenue/cost/profit for the old board; this set re-teaches those topics only where they appear as separate 4BS1 units (1.1, 4.1, 4.2) with new fictional contexts and IGCSE-style questions. No Drive material adapted.

lessons.title: Why businesses exist: needs, wants and enterprise
objectives: Explain the purpose of a business and distinguish needs from wants and goods from services
Define enterprise and entrepreneur and describe what an entrepreneur does

keywords.def: an organisation that provides goods or services to meet customer needs and wants
a person who takes the risk of starting and running a business
something a person must have to live, such as food, water and shelter
something a person would like but could live without
the skill of seeing an opportunity and organising resources to use it

starter: Name two things you bought or used this week. Who made or supplied each one?
Is a coat in winter a need or a want? Explain.
Give one difference between a good and a service.

teach.heading: Bismillah: business as halal earning
bullets: Trade is encouraged in Islam when done honestly
The Prophet (peace be upon him) was a trader
We study business to understand how money and work connect
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Point out that Qur'an 2:275 says Allah has permitted trade, and that the Prophet (peace be upon him) worked as a merchant before prophethood. A reported saying in Sahih al-Bukhari is that no one has eaten better food than what he earned by the work of his own hands. Set the tone: we learn business skills so we can earn honestly and serve people well.

teach.heading: The purpose of business
bullets: Businesses meet customers' needs and wants
They produce goods or provide services
They add value to resources
They aim to earn a reward for the owner
teach.note: Ask: what is the point of a business? Draw out that it takes inputs (resources) and turns them into something people will pay for. Goods are physical (a loaf of bread); services are not (a haircut). Many businesses sell both, such as a restaurant.

teach.heading: Needs and wants
bullets: Needs: food, water, shelter, clothing
Wants: designer trainers, the latest phone
Wants change; needs stay similar
Scarcity forces people to choose
teach.note: Common misconception: the same item cannot be both. A phone may be a want for one person but close to a need for a person who runs a business from it. Introduce scarcity: resources are limited, so choices must be made, and businesses compete to be chosen.

teach.heading: Enterprise and entrepreneurs
bullets: Enterprise: spotting and acting on an opportunity
An entrepreneur organises the resources
They make decisions and take risks
They hope to earn profit as a reward
teach.note: Link to the four things an entrepreneur brings together: land, labour, capital and enterprise (the factors of production, though the Edexcel spec focuses on the entrepreneur's role). Ask pupils to name a young entrepreneur they know of. Stress that entrepreneurs are not only huge names; a market stall owner is one.

teach.heading: Worked example: Bilal's tutoring service
bullets: Bilal sees pupils struggling with GCSE maths
He organises a room, resources and himself
He sells a service at 12 pounds an hour
He takes the risk that pupils may not come
teach.note: Walk through each bullet and label it: opportunity, resources, service not good, price, risk. Ask: what would Bilal's want or need be for his customers? (Parents want grades; pupils need to pass.) This models the 'identify, apply' skill for later exam answers.

practice: Sort into needs or wants and goods or services: bottled water, a mobile phone contract, a plumber's visit, a pair of football boots.
Explain in two sentences what an entrepreneur does, using the words 'risk' and 'resources'.
A halal bakery sells bread and also offers cake-decorating classes. Identify one good and one service it provides.
independent: Make a table of five local businesses, stating the need or want each meets and whether it sells goods, services or both.
Explain why a business needs customers in order to survive (4 marks style: identify, then explain two linked points).
Write a short paragraph on whether a market stall owner counts as an entrepreneur. Justify your answer.
exit: Define 'entrepreneur' in one sentence.
Give one example of a want and one of a need that a business could meet.
lessons.homework: Interview a family member or neighbour who runs or has run a business and write five sentences on why they started it.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: card sort of needs/wants and goods/services with picture support and a word bank. Stretch: explain why the same product could be a need for one customer and a want for another.

lessons.title: Risk and reward: the entrepreneur's decision
objectives: Describe the risks and rewards of starting a business
Analyse why entrepreneurs start a business and the qualities they need

keywords.def: the chance that something goes wrong, such as losing money
the benefit an entrepreneur gains from running a business
revenue minus total costs
when a business cannot pay its debts and has to close
being your own boss and making your own decisions

starter: Define 'entrepreneur'.
Give one example of a want a new business could meet.
What is the difference between a good and a service?

teach.heading: Why start a business?
bullets: To earn profit and financial security
To be your own boss
To follow a passion or idea
To meet a need in the community
teach.note: Ask pupils to rank these motives. Stress that profit is not the only reason: many entrepreneurs want independence or to help others. In Islam, a business that serves the community's genuine needs with honest dealing is a form of worship when the intention is right.

teach.heading: The risks of starting up
bullets: Losing the money you invested
No guaranteed wage or sick pay
Long working hours and stress
Business failure and debt
teach.note: Most new businesses do not last for many years; do not quote a precise statistic unless you have the source. Ask: why is a regular job less risky? (Fixed wage, holiday pay, employer takes the risk.)

teach.heading: The rewards of success
bullets: Profit, which belongs to the owner
Independence and control
Personal satisfaction and pride
Business success and growth
teach.note: Reward is not guaranteed. Link risk and reward: usually the higher the risk, the higher the possible reward. Connect to the principle that profit in Islam should come from real trade and shared risk, not from guaranteed gains.

teach.heading: Entrepreneurial qualities
bullets: Willingness to take risks
Creativity and new ideas
Determination and hard work
Good communication and honesty
teach.note: Edexcel questions often ask you to identify a quality from a case study. Practice quoting: 'Aisha keeps trying after her first order was refused, showing determination'. Add honesty (sidq and amanah) as a key quality of a trusted trader.

teach.heading: Worked example: Aisha's cupcake business
bullets: She spends 600 pounds on equipment
She earns 1,500 pounds in her first month
Costs are 900 pounds, so profit is 600 pounds
A bad month could mean a loss
teach.note: Work out: profit = revenue minus costs = 1,500 - 900 = 600 pounds. Then ask: what would she have if sales were 700 pounds? (A loss of 200 pounds.) Show that the same decision can give profit or loss, which is risk.

practice: List two risks and two rewards for someone leaving a job to open a halal grocery shop.
Aisha's revenue is 1,200 pounds and her costs are 1,350 pounds. Calculate her profit or loss.
Which entrepreneurial quality does a person show if they redesign a product after customer complaints? Explain.
independent: Explain two reasons why someone might start their own business instead of working for an employer.
Explain one way risk and reward are connected for a new business (4 marks style).
Write a paragraph assessing whether the rewards of owning a business outweigh the risks for a school leaver.
exit: State two risks of starting a business.
Calculate profit if revenue is 2,000 pounds and costs are 1,450 pounds.
lessons.homework: Choose a real small business you know and write six sentences on its likely risks and rewards for the owner.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: risk and reward sorting cards with symbols; sentence starter 'A risk is... A reward is...'. Stretch: evaluate whether profit is always the main reward.

lessons.title: The dynamic business world: new ideas and adding value
objectives: Explain why business ideas come from changes in technology and consumer wants
Describe ways a business can add value to compete

keywords.def: always changing
no longer wanted or used because something better has replaced it
the difference between the cost of inputs and the selling price of the product
a feature that makes a product different from competitors
a name, logo or image that identifies a business and its products

starter: State two risks of starting a business.
State two rewards of starting a business.
Name one quality of a successful entrepreneur.

teach.heading: Business never stands still
bullets: Customer tastes change
Technology creates new options
Old products can become obsolete
Businesses must adapt or lose customers
teach.note: Ask pupils: how did people listen to music 20 years ago compared with today? Use this to show products becoming obsolete and new markets appearing. Keep examples general to avoid factual error.

teach.heading: Where new ideas come from
bullets: New technology: apps, online selling
Changing lifestyles: busy people want convenience
Gaps in the market
Improving an existing product
teach.note: Misconception: ideas must be completely new. Most successful ideas are improvements or new combinations. Ask pupils to spot a gap at school or in their community, such as a quick halal breakfast option.

teach.heading: Adding value
bullets: Added value = selling price minus cost of inputs
Convenience, quality, design
Branding and customer service
Higher value allows higher prices or more sales
teach.note: Show a worked example: a baker spends 0.40 pounds on ingredients per loaf and sells it for 2.20 pounds. Added value is 1.80 pounds. Ask how they could raise it (better packaging, a local brand, home delivery).

teach.heading: Unique selling point
bullets: A USP is what makes you different
It can be price, quality or service
It should matter to customers
It must be honest, not exaggerated
teach.note: Stress the honesty point: Islam condemns deception in trade. A reported saying in Sahih Muslim states that whoever cheats us is not one of us. A USP must be true; false claims also break consumer law.

teach.heading: Why businesses fail
bullets: Not enough customers
Poor cash management
Poor quality or service
Failing to change with the market
teach.note: Link back to dynamic markets. Ask pupils to pick the most likely reason for failure for a new bookshop. Accept different answers if they justify them with business reasoning.

practice: A café buys ingredients for 1.10 pounds and sells a smoothie for 3.60 pounds. Calculate the added value.
Give two ways a trainer shop could add value without cutting its price.
Explain what makes a product obsolete, with one example.
independent: Choose a product and list three changes in consumer wants or technology that could make it obsolete.
Explain two ways a new business could create a unique selling point (4 marks style).
Write a paragraph: is adding value more important than low prices for a new small business? Justify your view.
exit: Define 'added value'.
State one way a business can add value to its product.
lessons.homework: Pick a local shop or online seller and write a short note on its USP and two ways it adds value.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: add-value calculation scaffold with ready-made subtraction frames. Stretch: explain how added value affects both price and profit.

lessons.title: Customer needs and market segmentation
objectives: Explain why understanding customer needs is vital for a new business
Describe market segmentation and the main ways of segmenting a market

keywords.def: the things customers require from a product, such as price, quality and choice
where buyers and sellers meet to trade a good or service
dividing a market into groups of customers with similar characteristics
characteristics of a population such as age, gender and income
the group of customers a business aims its product at

starter: Define 'added value'.
What is a USP?
Give one reason why products become obsolete.

teach.heading: What do customers want?
bullets: Price: is it affordable?
Quality: does it last and work?
Choice: are there options?
Convenience: is it easy to buy and use?
teach.note: Make clear these are the Edexcel customer needs. Ask pupils to rank them for a school lunch and then for a laptop to see priorities change. Add that for Muslim customers, halal certification can be an essential need, not an optional extra.

teach.heading: Why identify customers?
bullets: Avoid wasting money on the wrong product
Match the product to customers' needs
Decide price and promotion sensibly
Build loyalty and repeat sales
teach.note: A common error is saying 'everyone is a customer'. Explain that small businesses have limited money, so they must focus. Ask what would happen if a modest-fashion shop advertised to everyone in the country.

teach.heading: Market segmentation
bullets: Split a market into groups
Each group has similar needs
A business can then target the right group
More effective than selling to everyone
teach.note: Define segmentation clearly, then target market. A segment is one part; the target market is the segment(s) chosen.

teach.heading: Ways to segment
bullets: Demographics: age, gender, income, family size
Location: urban, rural, region
Lifestyle: sports fans, busy parents, vegetarians
Income: budget, mid-range, premium
teach.note: Give a worked example: a gym could segment by age (teenagers, adults, over 60s), lifestyle (competitive athletes or relaxers) and location. Ask pupils to produce a segment for a halal ready-meal brand: busy professionals aged 25 to 40 in cities.

teach.heading: Worked example: Zayd's sportswear
bullets: Segment: boys aged 11 to 16 who play football
Need: affordable, hard-wearing kit
Place: online and school team orders
Promotion: social media and local clubs
teach.note: Use this to model a short analysis answer: identify segment, give reason, link to marketing choice. Ask pupils to find a second segment Zayd could add and why.

practice: Name two customer needs a family would consider when choosing a restaurant.
A business sells prayer mats online. Identify two ways it could segment its market.
Explain why a bookshop might target students rather than the whole population.
independent: Choose a product of your own and describe its target market using at least three types of segmentation.
Explain two benefits to a small business of segmenting its market (4 marks style).
Write a paragraph assessing whether price or quality is more important to customers of a school uniform supplier.
exit: Define 'market segmentation'.
Give two ways a market can be segmented.
lessons.homework: Look at an advert and write five sentences identifying its target market and the evidence for it.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: matching cards for segment type and example. Stretch: explain why segments can overlap and how a business decides which one to prioritise.

lessons.title: Market research: finding out what customers want
objectives: Explain the purpose of market research and distinguish primary from secondary research
Evaluate the usefulness of research methods and data types for a small business

keywords.def: collecting information about customers, competitors and the market
new information collected first-hand for a specific purpose
information that already exists, collected by someone else
opinions and feelings that are not numbers
numerical data that can be counted and analysed

starter: Define 'target market'.
List three ways to segment a market.
Why is it risky to sell to 'everyone'?

teach.heading: Why do market research?
bullets: Find out what customers want
Reduce the risk of failure
Learn about competitors
Decide on price and location
teach.note: Link to risk from lesson 2. Ask: would you open a shop without knowing if anybody wants what you sell? Research cannot remove risk but it reduces it.

teach.heading: Primary research
bullets: Surveys and questionnaires
Interviews and focus groups
Observation and product trials
Specific to your needs but costs time and money
teach.note: Explain each method with a quick example. Teach that a good questionnaire has clear, unbiased questions. Misconception: online surveys are always cheap; they are, but responses may not represent the target market.

teach.heading: Secondary research
bullets: Government statistics and reports
Market reports and trade magazines
Websites and social media
Cheaper and quicker but may be out of date
teach.note: Emphasise that secondary data was collected for another purpose, so it may not fit. Ask pupils how a new halal food company could use government population data on where Muslims live (as an indicator of demand).

teach.heading: Qualitative or quantitative?
bullets: Quantitative: 62 percent prefer delivery
Qualitative: 'I like the friendly service'
Numbers show scale; opinions show why
Most businesses use both
teach.note: Practise classification with quick examples. Tell pupils that quantitative data is easier to analyse and compare but does not explain why people think as they do.

teach.heading: Sampling and reliability
bullets: A sample is a smaller group from the target market
A larger, random sample is more reliable
Biased questions give poor results
Check how recent the data is
teach.note: Worked example: a café asks 20 friends and 18 love the idea. Why is that unreliable? (Too small, friends are biased, not representative.) A better sample: 200 people selected at random from the target area.

practice: Classify each as primary or secondary: a survey of 50 students, a government census report, a trade magazine article, a focus group.
A new halal pizza takeaway wants to know prices customers will pay. Suggest one primary method and explain why.
Explain why asking only friends and family may lead to poor research results.
independent: Write five questions for a questionnaire for a new hijab and modest-fashion brand, including at least one qualitative and one quantitative question.
Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of secondary research for a start-up (4 marks style).
Write a paragraph: should a new business rely on primary or secondary research? Justify your recommendation.
exit: State the difference between primary and secondary research.
Give one example of quantitative data.
lessons.homework: Design a short survey of five questions for your family about a product idea and write a brief note on how you would use the results.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: pre-written survey question frames. Stretch: evaluate how sample size and bias affect decision-making.

lessons.title: Competition and market mapping
objectives: Explain how competition affects a small business
Interpret a market map to identify a gap in the market

keywords.def: a business selling similar products to the same customers
a diagram showing where competing products sit, for example on price and quality
an unmet customer need that no business is yet supplying
something that lets a business perform better than its rivals
a business's sales as a percentage of total sales in the market

starter: Define primary research.
Give an example of qualitative data.
State one problem with a very small sample.

teach.heading: Understanding competition
bullets: Rivals sell to the same customers
Direct and indirect competitors
Competition can lower prices
Competition can force higher quality
teach.note: Distinguish direct competitors (another halal burger kiosk) from indirect (a sandwich shop). Ask whether competition is good for customers. Usually yes, but it makes survival harder for small firms.

teach.heading: Effects on small businesses
bullets: Lower profits if prices are cut
Need to stand out with a USP
Risk of losing customers
May push the business to improve
teach.note: Edexcel often asks for the impact of competition on a business. Model a chain of reasoning: new rival opens, customers switch, sales fall, profit falls, owner must cut costs or add value.

teach.heading: Market mapping
bullets: A grid with two features, e.g. price and quality
Each competitor is plotted as a point
Gaps show unmet needs
Crowded areas show strong competition
teach.note: Draw a 2 by 2 grid: price (low to high) on one axis, quality (low to high) on the other. Plot four sandwich shops. Ask: where is the gap? Misconception: a gap always means opportunity. It may mean there are no customers there.

teach.heading: Using the map
bullets: Spot a gap such as high quality at low price
Check there is demand through research
Position your product clearly
Review as competitors change
teach.note: Emphasise that the gap must be tested. Link to market research. Competition should be fair; Islam supports healthy competition in good deeds, and honest rivalry, not spreading false rumours about a competitor.

teach.heading: Worked example: Maryam's bakery
bullets: Rivals: supermarket (low price, medium quality), artisan bakery (high price, high quality)
Gap: medium price, high quality, halal
Maryam positions her bakery in that gap
She tests demand with a survey
teach.note: Plot the three businesses on the board and show the gap. Ask what could go wrong (e.g. customers may not pay medium price for high quality) and how she can find out.

practice: Name one direct and one indirect competitor for a halal fast-food kiosk.
On a price/quality grid, a business has high price and low quality. Why is this likely to struggle?
Give two ways a small business can compete without lowering price.
independent: Draw a market map for four local food outlets and identify a possible gap.
Explain two ways a new competitor could affect an existing small shop (4 marks style).
Write a paragraph assessing whether competition is more of a threat or an opportunity for a start-up.
exit: Define 'gap in the market'.
State one way competition can affect a small business.
lessons.homework: Choose a product and plot at least five competing brands on a price/quality market map; label any gaps.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: pre-drawn grid and cut-out business cards to position. Stretch: assess why a gap in the market may not be profitable.

lessons.unit: Unit 3: Putting a business idea into practice
lessons.title: Business aims and objectives
objectives: Distinguish between business aims and objectives
Explain financial and non-financial aims of a new business and why they differ

keywords.def: the long-term goal a business wants to achieve
a specific target that helps achieve an aim, often with a number and a date
keeping the business going, especially in the first year
a goal to benefit people or the community, not only to make profit
having enough stable income to pay bills with confidence

starter: What is a market map?
State two effects of competition on a business.
Define 'competitive advantage'.

teach.heading: Aims versus objectives
bullets: Aim: where the business wants to be
Objective: a specific step to get there
Objectives are measurable
Objectives have a time limit
teach.note: Give an example: Aim: become the favourite local halal bakery. Objective: sell 500 loaves a week by next June. Ask pupils to turn a vague aim into an objective with a number and a date.

teach.heading: Financial aims
bullets: Survival, especially for new firms
Profit
Sales and sales growth
Market share and financial security
teach.note: Explain that survival is the first aim for most start-ups. Profit comes later. Show that sales growth is not the same as profit; selling more at a loss does not help.

teach.heading: Non-financial aims
bullets: Social objectives: helping the community
Personal satisfaction and challenge
Independence and control
Ethical aims, such as fair treatment of staff
teach.note: Link to Islamic ethics: Qur'an 4:29 permits trade based on mutual consent, and honest dealing is part of faith. A business with social objectives, such as donating a percentage to a local food bank, can still make a profit. Ask whether social aims reduce profit.

teach.heading: Why aims differ
bullets: Owner's personality and motives
Age and stage of the business
Competition and the economy
Size: sole trader or larger firm
teach.note: Use two cases: a new sole trader (survival and independence) and an established firm (growth and market share). Ask why a start-up cannot easily aim for 30 percent market share.

teach.heading: SMART objectives
bullets: Specific, Measurable, Achievable
Realistic and Time-bound
Helps judge success
Motivates staff and owner
teach.note: Work through a SMART objective: 'Increase monthly sales from 2,000 to 2,400 pounds within six months' (that is a 20 percent increase). Check pupils can calculate 20 percent of 2,000.

practice: Turn this aim into an objective: 'We want to be well known in our area.'
Sort into financial or non-financial: survival, helping the community, profit, independence.
Explain why a new business might choose survival as its first aim.
independent: Write one aim and two SMART objectives for a new halal catering company.
Explain two reasons why aims may differ between a new sole trader and a large company (4 marks style).
Write a paragraph assessing whether profit should be the most important aim for a small business.
exit: State the difference between an aim and an objective.
Give one financial and one non-financial aim.
lessons.homework: Research a small business online and write five sentences on its likely aims and how you can tell.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: aim/objective sorting activity and SMART checklist. Stretch: evaluate whether non-financial aims could harm a business's survival.

lessons.unit: Unit 3: Putting a business idea into practice
lessons.title: Revenue, costs and profit
objectives: Calculate revenue, total costs and profit or loss
Distinguish fixed from variable costs and explain how interest affects a business

keywords.def: the money a business receives from selling goods or services (price x quantity)
costs that stay the same however much is produced, such as rent
costs that change with output, such as ingredients
fixed costs plus variable costs
revenue minus total costs; if negative it is a loss

starter: Define a SMART objective.
Give one financial aim and one non-financial aim.
Why is survival important for a new business?

teach.heading: Revenue
bullets: Revenue = price x quantity sold
Also called turnover or sales revenue
Revenue is not profit
Example: 400 bars at 3 pounds = 1,200 pounds
teach.note: Misconception: revenue and profit are the same. Ask: if you sell 400 bars for 3 pounds each and spend 1,300 pounds, did you profit? (No, a loss of 100 pounds.)

teach.heading: Fixed and variable costs
bullets: Fixed: rent, insurance, salaries
Variable: ingredients, packaging
Total costs = fixed + variable
Variable costs rise with output
teach.note: Hold up a cup: its cup and ingredients are variable costs; the café rent is fixed. Ask pupils to classify more examples. Variable cost = variable cost per unit x number of units.

teach.heading: Calculating profit
bullets: Profit = revenue - total costs
Negative profit is a loss
Check units and months match
Show working in exams
teach.note: Present the worked example fully on the board.

teach.heading: Worked example: Yusuf's date-and-oat bars
bullets: Price 3 pounds, 400 bars sold
Revenue = 3 x 400 = 1,200 pounds
Variable cost 1.20 per bar = 480 pounds
Fixed costs 240; total 720; profit 480 pounds
teach.note: Write out each step. Check: 240 + 480 = 720; 1,200 - 720 = 480. Ask: what happens if Yusuf sells only 150 bars? Revenue 450, variable 180, total 420, profit 30. Show that costs do not fall in proportion.

teach.heading: Interest and honest pricing
bullets: Interest is the cost of borrowing money
Higher borrowing raises costs
Muslim entrepreneurs avoid riba (interest)
Halal options: savings, partners, profit-sharing
teach.note: Present as a note, not exam content. Qur'an 2:275 states that Allah has permitted trade and forbidden riba. Many Muslim business owners start with savings or partners sharing risk and profit. Also tie to honest pricing: a fair price and accurate weights and measures (Qur'an 83:1-3 warns against cheating in measure).

practice: Calculate revenue: a stall sells 250 scarves at 8 pounds each.
A café has rent of 500 pounds a month and variable costs of 2 pounds per drink. Calculate total costs for 600 drinks.
Using your answers, calculate the profit if the café sells 600 drinks at 3.50 pounds.
independent: A business sells 300 notebooks at 4 pounds. Fixed costs 350 pounds, variable cost 1.50 per notebook. Calculate revenue, total costs and profit.
Explain two reasons why a business might make a loss even if sales are high (4 marks style).
Write a paragraph assessing whether a start-up should focus on cutting costs or increasing revenue.
exit: Calculate revenue: 120 items sold at 15 pounds each.
Give one fixed cost and one variable cost for a bakery.
lessons.homework: Create your own business with a price and costs, and calculate its revenue, total costs and profit for one month.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: worked calculation frames with boxes to fill. Stretch: calculate profit if price rises 10 percent and sales fall 5 percent.

lessons.title: Business aims and objectives: why a business exists and where it is heading
lessons.bigQuestion: If a business makes no profit, has it failed?
objectives: Distinguish an aim from an objective
Describe financial aims: survival, profit, sales, market share, financial security
Describe non-financial aims and explain why objectives change over time
successCriteria: All: define aim and objective and name three aims
Most: match an aim to a business and say whether it is financial
Some: explain how a change in market conditions or legislation would change an objective
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: percentage market share and percentage change in sales
lessons.smsc: Moral: honesty and fairness as part of how success is measured; halal earning as a purpose beyond profit

keywords.def: the long-term goal of a business
a measurable target that helps a business reach its aim
staying in business, the main aim of most new firms
revenue minus total costs
a firm's sales as a percentage of total sales in the market
having enough money to keep going through hard times

starter: Bismillah. Name two businesses on your road. What do you think each one wants to achieve?
What is the difference between a good and a service? Give one example of each.
A shop sold 400 items at 5 pounds each. Calculate its revenue.

teach.heading: Aims versus objectives
bullets: An aim is the long-term goal
An objective is a measurable target
Objectives are the steps towards the aim
Good objectives have a number and a date
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Use a running example: Noor's Bakery in a fictional town. Aim: to be the best-known bakery in the town. Objective: to sell 1,200 loaves a week by next March. Ask pupils which is the aim and which is the objective, and why the objective is easier to check. Misconception: the two words are not interchangeable in the exam; an aim is broad, an objective is specific and measurable.

teach.heading: Financial aims
bullets: Survival: vital for a new business
Profit: revenue minus costs
Sales: revenue and sales volume growth
Market share: share of total market sales
Financial security: a cash cushion for hard times
teach.note: Go through each aim with a fictional example. Survival: the first-year coffee kiosk. Profit: a firm that wants 20,000 pounds a year. Sales growth: a clothes shop wants sales up 10 per cent. Market share: if the market is worth 2 million pounds and Noor's sells 200,000 pounds, its share is 10 per cent. Financial security: owner can pay wages for three months even if sales fall. Ask: which aim matters most to a business in its first six months? Most pupils will say survival; push on why.

teach.heading: Worked example: market share
teach.note: Model the calculation slowly. Emphasise that market share needs the total market figure, which the exam will give. Then ask what a rise from 10 to 12 per cent would mean for the firm. Remind pupils that this is a quantitative skill: show the working, include the percentage sign.

model.problem: Noor's Bakery sold 240,000 pounds of bread in a year. All bakeries in the town sold 1,600,000 pounds. Calculate Noor's market share.
steps: Write the formula: market share = firm's sales divided by total market sales, times 100
Multiply by 100 to give a percentage

teach.heading: Non-financial aims
bullets: Social objectives: help the community or environment
Personal satisfaction: enjoying the work
Challenge: testing yourself in a new venture
Independence and control: being your own boss
teach.note: Explain that not every owner chases the highest profit. A charity-minded business might give some of its earnings to a local school. Link to the Islamic ethos: many Muslim business owners aim to earn halal income and deal honestly, and may give charity from profit. Do not state rulings; invite the class to discuss and the teacher can expand. Ask: can a business have both financial and non-financial aims? Draw out that it usually does.

teach.heading: Check: financial or non-financial?
teach.note: Hinge question on mini-whiteboards. Show answer letters at once. The trap is option C: sales growth is financial. Option B is a non-financial social aim.

check.q: Hamza opens a fictional garden centre. He says, 'My first aim is to still be trading in two years.' Which aim is this?
check.why: Staying in business is survival, a financial aim. Market share needs a percentage of the market; a social objective helps the community.

teach.heading: Why objectives change
bullets: Market conditions: new competitors or falling demand
Technology: online selling changes what is possible
Performance: beating or missing targets
Legislation: new laws, such as a higher minimum wage
Internal reasons: new owner or new managers
teach.note: Give the Noor's Bakery story: a supermarket opens next door (market conditions), so the objective moves from growing sales to keeping loyal customers. Then a new law raises minimum wage (legislation) so profit objective is lowered. Ask pupils to give an example for each of the five reasons. Note that the exam can ask them to explain why a given objective might change in the context of a given firm.

practice: Hamza's garden centre had revenue of 90,000 pounds. The whole market in the area was 600,000 pounds. Calculate his market share.
Write one aim and one measurable objective for a fictional school uniform shop opening in September.
State two reasons why Noor's Bakery might change its objective from growth to survival.
independent: Core: Sort ten aims (for example: to be the largest, to enjoy the work, to help local people, to survive, to earn 30,000 pounds) into financial and non-financial.
Extend: Explain two reasons why a new coffee kiosk might change its objectives after six months.
Stretch: Exam style (6 marks, Explain): 'A new business should always make survival its main aim.' Explain two reasons for and one against, and give a short conclusion.
exit: Define the term market share.
Give one financial and one non-financial aim for a business of your choice.
Big question: if a business makes no profit, has it failed? Answer in two sentences.
lessons.homework: Find a real small business near you and write its likely aim and one objective, saying whether each is financial.
lessons.send: SEND: give a card sort with aims already labelled as financial or non-financial for support. EAL: pre-teach aim, objective, survival with images. Stretch: ask pupils to rank five aims for a start-up and justify the order.

lessons.title: Sole traders and partnerships: owning a small business
lessons.bigQuestion: Would you start a business alone or with a partner?
objectives: Describe a sole trader and a partnership
Compare them by risk, ownership, limited liability, control, finance and use of profits
Judge which suits a small business
successCriteria: All: define sole trader and partnership and state one advantage of each
Most: explain unlimited liability and why it is a risk
Some: justify the better form for a given business
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: sharing profit in a ratio
lessons.smsc: Moral: trust and honest dealing between partners; keeping promises (amanah) in a partnership agreement

keywords.def: a business owned and run by one person
a business owned by two to twenty people who share risk and profit
owners are personally responsible for all the debts of the business
a written agreement setting out how partners share profit and decisions

starter: Define the terms aim and objective.
Give one financial and one non-financial business aim.
Noor's Bakery has 18% market share. Total market sales are 500,000 pounds. How much did Noor's sell?

teach.heading: Sole traders
bullets: One owner, often the only worker
Keeps all the profit
Makes decisions without consulting others
Unlimited liability: personal assets at risk
Finance usually comes from own savings or loans
teach.note: Use fictional Sami, a mobile phone repairer. He decides everything, keeps all profit, and can start quickly. Risk: if he owes 15,000 pounds and the business cannot pay, creditors can take his car and savings. Ask: why is it hard for him to grow? Draw out limited finance and one pair of hands. Point out that sole traders are very common among small businesses.

teach.heading: Partnerships
bullets: Two or more owners, usually up to 20
Profits shared as agreed, often in a ratio
More skills and more capital than one person
Unlimited liability, and each partner can be liable for the others' debts
A deed of partnership prevents arguments
teach.note: Sami joins Yusuf, a web designer, to make a repair-and-web shop. Discuss benefits: two lots of savings, two skills, shared workload. Drawbacks: disagreements, sharing profit, and being responsible for the other's mistakes. Stress the written agreement. Link to trust: Muslims are encouraged to honour agreements; invite pupils to say why a clear written agreement shows honesty and prevents harm. Avoid quoting any text.

teach.heading: Worked example: sharing partnership profit
teach.note: Walk through the ratio calculation. Check that pupils add the ratio parts first. Ask what happens to each partner's share if profit falls to 18,000 pounds. Then discuss fairness: is a 3:2 split fair if both work the same hours? Pupils should say the deed of partnership decides.

model.problem: Sami and Yusuf share profit in the ratio 3:2. Their profit is 30,000 pounds. How much does each receive?

teach.heading: Compare: sole trader and partnership
teach.note: Use as a revision grid. Ask pupils to cover one column and recall the other. Note control: a sole trader has full control; partners must agree. Neither has limited liability. Exam tip: when asked which is better, refer to the business in the question, not generic points.

teach.heading: Check: liability
teach.note: Mini-whiteboards. Answer B. Distractor A is the limited-liability idea that belongs to companies; C is a confusion with control.

check.q: Sami's business owes 8,000 pounds and cannot pay. What does unlimited liability mean for him?
options: He only loses the money he put in
His own possessions could be used to pay the debt
His customers must pay the debt
check.why: Unlimited liability means the owner is personally responsible. Only limited-liability owners lose just their investment.

teach.heading: Which form suits which business?
bullets: A one-person market stall: sole trader
A two-dentist surgery needing equipment: partnership
Ask: how much capital? how much risk?
Ask: does the owner want control?
teach.note: Practise judging. Give three quick scenarios and take votes. Emphasise that the correct answer depends on size, finance needed and the owner's preference. In an exam justification answer pupils must use the context and reach a clear decision.

practice: Maryam and Aisha share profit in the ratio 1:3. Profit is 24,000 pounds. Calculate each share.
State two advantages of a partnership over a sole trader.
Explain why a deed of partnership is useful.
independent: Core: Complete a table comparing a sole trader and partnership for a fictional hair salon.
Extend: Explain two risks for a sole trader who owns a fictional bicycle repair shop.
Stretch: Justify (6 marks): Sami has 6,000 pounds savings and wants to open a computer shop needing 25,000 pounds. Should he stay a sole trader or form a partnership? Use the figures.
exit: Define unlimited liability.
Give one benefit and one drawback of a partnership.
Big question: would you start alone or with a partner? One reason.
lessons.homework: Interview someone you know who runs a small business and note what ownership form it has and why.
lessons.send: SEND: give the ratio sharing steps as a prompt card. EAL: pair 'liable' with 'responsible for debts'. Stretch: compare the position if a partner disappears and leaves debts.

lessons.title: Companies and public corporations: limited liability
lessons.bigQuestion: Why would an owner want their house protected from business debts?
objectives: Describe private limited companies, public limited companies and public corporations
Explain limited liability and shares
Compare forms by risk, control, finance and use of profit
successCriteria: All: define limited liability and name three business forms
Most: compare a private and public limited company
Some: explain why a growing business might change its form
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: dividends as a share of profit; percentage ownership
lessons.smsc: Moral: transparency and honest accounts when the public can buy shares

keywords.def: owners can lose only the money they invested
shares sold privately, not to the public; has limited liability
can sell shares to the public on a stock exchange
an owner of a company who holds shares
a share of profit paid to shareholders
a business owned and controlled by the government

starter: Define unlimited liability.
Give two features of a partnership.
Sami and Yusuf's business owes 20,000 pounds. Who is responsible?

teach.heading: Limited liability and shares
bullets: A company is a separate legal person from its owners
Owners (shareholders) can lose only what they invested
Money is raised by selling shares
Profits are paid as dividends
teach.note: Use the fictional Zayn's Solar Ltd. Four shareholders invest 10,000 each. If it owes 100,000 and collapses, each can lose only the 10,000 invested, not house or savings. Contrast with sole trader. Do not teach company accounts; stay at concept level. For Muslim pupils, note that investing in a company by buying shares is discussed by scholars, and the teacher may expand on which businesses and structures are considered permissible; do not give rulings.

teach.heading: Private and public limited companies
teach.note: Compare table. Key facts: Ltd shares are not for sale to the general public and are sold only with the agreement of existing owners, so owners keep control. A plc may sell shares to the public, raising big sums but risking takeover and has to publish more information. Ask: why might Zayn's Solar stay a Ltd? Answer: keeps control, avoids disclosure.

teach.heading: Public corporations
bullets: Owned by the government
Run for public benefit, not only profit
Funded by taxes and its own sales
Example: a fictional national railway corporation
teach.note: A public corporation is owned by the state and run by appointed managers; objectives are often public service. Avoid stating that a specific current organisation is or is not one unless sure; use the fictional Nile Valley Railways Corporation as the model. Ask: why might a government keep a railway public? Draw out service to everyone, jobs and national importance.

teach.heading: Worked example: dividends
teach.note: Take pupils through the dividend per share method. Ask what happens to dividend per share if profit distributed doubles. Check they can find the percentage owned: Zainab holds 2,000 of 10,000 shares = 20 per cent.

model.problem: Zayn's Solar Ltd has 10,000 shares. It pays 15,000 pounds in total dividends. Zainab owns 2,000 shares. How much does she receive?
steps: Dividend per share = 15,000 divided by 10,000 = 1.50 pounds
Check: she owns 20 per cent and 20 per cent of 15,000 is 3,000

teach.heading: Check: which form?
teach.note: Answer C. A is wrong because public limited companies sell shares to the public; B because limited liability protects personal assets; D because a sole trader cannot sell shares.

check.q: A business wants to raise 5 million pounds by selling shares on the stock exchange. Which form must it be?
check.why: Only a plc can sell shares to the public on a stock exchange.

teach.heading: Choosing the right form
bullets: Small, low risk, one owner: sole trader
Two professionals: partnership
Wants protection from debt: limited company
Large, needs big capital: plc
teach.note: Run a decision tree activity. Pupils decide for three scenarios. Evaluate: limited liability protects owners but a company has more legal paperwork. In the exam, use evidence from the given business.

practice: Eight friends each invest 5,000 pounds in a Ltd. It collapses owing 200,000 pounds. What is the most each friend can lose?
State two differences between a Ltd and a plc.
Explain one reason a government might run a business as a public corporation.
independent: Core: Match six features (for example 'owned by the state', 'shares sold on the stock exchange') to the correct form.
Extend: Explain two advantages of limited liability for the owner of Zayn's Solar.
Stretch: Evaluate (8 marks): 'Becoming a plc is always the best way for a successful Ltd to grow.' Use pros, cons and a judgement.
exit: Define limited liability in one sentence.
Name the form of business owned by the government.
Big question answer: why would an owner want protection from business debts?
lessons.homework: Choose a business you know and decide whether it is more likely a sole trader, Ltd or plc; give two reasons.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a flowchart for choosing the form. EAL: create a glossary for shares, dividend, liability. Stretch: investigate the reasons a family firm might refuse to float.

lessons.title: Stakeholders, franchises, social enterprises and multinationals
lessons.bigQuestion: Who else cares whether a business succeeds, apart from the owner?
objectives: Identify stakeholders and shareholders and their interests
Describe franchises, social enterprises and multinationals
Judge which ownership form suits a business
successCriteria: All: name three stakeholders and what each wants
Most: describe a franchise and a social enterprise
Some: justify a franchise or social enterprise for a given situation
lessons.smsc: Social: community responsibility; Moral: fair dealing with all stakeholders

keywords.def: any person or group affected by or interested in a business
an owner of shares in a company
a business using another firm's brand and system in return for fees
the owner of the brand who sells the franchise
the person who buys and runs the franchise
a business run to achieve a social aim, with profits mainly reinvested
a business operating in more than one country

starter: Name the form of business that can sell shares to the public.
Define limited liability.
State one advantage of being a sole trader.

teach.heading: Stakeholders
bullets: Owners and shareholders: profit and dividends
Employees: pay, security and good conditions
Customers: quality and fair prices
Suppliers: prompt payment
Community and government: jobs, tax and safety
teach.note: Use the fictional Al-Noor Bakery Ltd. Ask pupils to say what each group wants and where interests clash: higher wages for workers versus higher dividends for shareholders. Stress that a shareholder is a type of stakeholder but not every stakeholder is a shareholder. Link to ethics: treating customers, workers and suppliers fairly and honestly is something Islamic teaching emphasises; the teacher may expand with the class's own knowledge.

teach.heading: Franchises
bullets: Franchisee pays a fee and a share of sales
Uses the franchisor's brand, products and training
Lower risk because the idea is proven
Less freedom and profit shared with the franchisor
teach.note: Use the fictional Burger Barn franchise. Franchisee pays 20,000 pounds to start and 5 per cent of sales. Ask: who benefits? The franchisor expands with less capital; the franchisee gets a known brand. Drawbacks: rules on menu and prices, fees reduce profit. Misconception: a franchisee is not an employee; they own and run their own business.

teach.heading: Worked example: franchise fees
teach.note: Model the calculation, then ask whether the franchise is worthwhile. Link to risk and the proven brand. Many pupils forget to subtract fees from profit.

model.problem: Layla runs a Burger Barn franchise. Annual sales are 240,000 pounds. She pays 5% of sales to the franchisor. Her other costs are 190,000 pounds. Calculate her profit.

teach.heading: Social enterprises and multinationals
teach.note: Contrast. A social enterprise is a business with a social purpose: for example the fictional Bright Start Cafe trains young unemployed people and reinvests profit. It still has to cover its costs. A multinational has operations in several countries: the fictional Orion Foods has factories in four countries. Benefits to the firm: new markets, cheaper labour; drawbacks: complex management. Detailed host-country effects come in Unit 1.5.

right.title: Multinational
points: Gains new markets and lower costs

teach.heading: Check: stakeholder or franchise?
teach.note: Answer C. Distractor A confuses a franchisor with a franchisee; B confuses with a shareholder.

check.q: Which statement about a franchisee is correct?
options: Owns the brand and sells licences
Is an employee of the franchisor
Pays fees to use a brand and runs the outlet
check.why: A franchisee runs the outlet using the franchisor's brand in return for fees.

teach.heading: Which ownership form fits?
bullets: Wants proven brand: franchise
Wants to help the community: social enterprise
Wants world markets: multinational
Match the choice to the owner's aims
teach.note: Use a quick-fire scenario set so pupils practise justification. For each ask for one benefit and one drawback. Remind them that in the exam, a recommendation needs a reason linked to the context.

practice: List three stakeholders of a school uniform shop and what each wants.
Burger Barn charges 6% of sales. A franchisee has sales of 150,000 pounds. Calculate the fee.
Describe one difference between a franchise and a social enterprise.
independent: Core: Complete a stakeholder grid for Al-Noor Bakery Ltd with two interests per group.
Extend: Explain how the interests of employees and shareholders may conflict.
Stretch: Justify (6 marks): Khalid has 30,000 pounds and wants to open a cafe. Should he start his own brand or buy a franchise costing 20,000 pounds plus 5% of sales?
exit: Define franchise.
Give one benefit of franchising to the franchisor.
Big question: name one stakeholder who is not the owner and what they want.
lessons.homework: Research a franchise business near you and note who the franchisor and franchisee are.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a stakeholder sorting grid. EAL: show examples of well-known franchises. Stretch: analyse why a social enterprise might struggle to grow.

lessons.title: Business sectors: primary, secondary and tertiary
lessons.bigQuestion: Where does the cost of a loaf of bread begin?
objectives: Classify businesses as primary, secondary or tertiary
Explain how the sectors depend on each other
Describe how the importance of sectors changes over time
successCriteria: All: name the three sectors with an example each
Most: classify mixed businesses correctly
Some: explain how the sectors form a chain
lessons.smsc: Social: respect for all kinds of work (dignity of labour)

keywords.def: businesses that extract or grow natural resources
businesses that make or build goods from raw materials
businesses that provide services
unprocessed resources used to make goods
the stages from raw material to the consumer

starter: Name two types of business ownership.
What is a franchise?
Name one stakeholder of a school.

teach.heading: Three sectors
bullets: Primary: farming, fishing, mining, oil extraction
Secondary: manufacturing, construction, food processing
Tertiary: shops, banks, schools, transport
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Give the bread chain: wheat grown by a fictional Delta Farm (primary), flour milled and bread baked by Golden Crust Bakery (secondary), sold by a supermarket (tertiary). Ask pupils to classify their own family's jobs. Misconception: a baker who also sells in the same shop is both secondary and tertiary.

teach.heading: Classify: sort the businesses
teach.note: Use as a quick sort. Pupils tick the sector for each. Point out the mixed cases (the garage and the bakery) to prompt discussion. Tell them classification depends on the main activity.

teach.heading: The chain of production
bullets: Each sector depends on the others
Primary supplies raw materials to secondary
Secondary supplies finished goods to tertiary
Tertiary delivers goods and services to customers
teach.note: Draw the chain with arrows. Ask what happens if the primary sector fails, for example a bad harvest. Link to price rises and shortages. Link to supply chains: a business is part of a chain, so its prices and quality depend on its suppliers.

teach.heading: Worked example: sector shares
teach.note: Model a simple sector calculation. Ask pupils what the figures suggest about a country's economy (mostly services). Remind them to give percentages with the working.

model.problem: Fictional Country Zeta has 2,000,000 workers: 200,000 primary, 400,000 secondary and the rest tertiary. Calculate the percentage in the tertiary sector.
model.answer: 70% of workers are in the tertiary sector

teach.heading: Check: classify
teach.note: Answer B. A mining firm extracts resources and is primary, a car factory secondary, a bank tertiary.

check.q: Which activity belongs to the secondary sector?
options: Turning flour into bread in a factory
check.why: Converting materials into goods is secondary; extracting and growing are primary; services are tertiary.

teach.heading: Changing importance of sectors
bullets: Richer countries have large tertiary sectors
Developing economies often rely more on primary
Technology moves jobs from secondary to tertiary
Businesses may move between sectors as they grow
teach.note: Discuss why the tertiary sector has grown: rising incomes, demand for services, machines doing factory work. Warn pupils not to state countries' exact percentages without data. A business can change: a fruit farm that starts a jam factory moves into secondary. Ask why a firm might do that (add value, higher prices).

practice: Classify: a gold mine, a furniture workshop, a hairdresser, a fishing boat.
Explain how a secondary sector business depends on the primary sector.
Name a business that operates in more than one sector and explain why.
independent: Core: Classify twelve fictional businesses and complete the chain for a cup of tea.
Extend: Explain one reason why a country's tertiary sector grows as its income rises.
Stretch: Analyse (6 marks): Hilltop Orchard grows apples (primary) and plans to open a jam factory and a cafe. Explain how this would change its sectors and risk.
exit: Name the three sectors.
Which sector is a bank in?
Big question: where does the cost of a loaf of bread begin?
lessons.homework: Trace the supply chain for one item you own (for example a pair of trainers) and label each sector.
lessons.send: SEND: use picture cards for sorting. EAL: pair each sector word with an action (extract, make, serve). Stretch: investigate why a country's main sector changes as it develops.

lessons.title: Location decisions: where should a business open?
lessons.bigQuestion: Would you open a bakery on a busy high street or an online shop from your home?
objectives: Describe the factors in location: market, labour, materials, competitors
Explain how the nature of the activity affects location
Explain the effect of the internet, legal controls and trade blocs on location
successCriteria: All: name four location factors
Most: explain how two factors would influence a given business
Some: justify a location and recommend one using evidence
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: industrial location and trade blocs
lessons.smsc: Social: the effect of a business on a local community and fair competition

keywords.def: nearness to something, such as customers or suppliers
buying and selling over the internet
a group of countries with agreed trading rules, often with reduced tariffs
the workers a business employs
legal approval needed to build or use premises
other firms selling similar goods or services

starter: Name the three business sectors.
Give an example of a secondary business.
What does a stakeholder want from a business? Give one example.

teach.heading: Key location factors
bullets: Market: close to customers
Labour: availability and skill, wage levels
Materials: near suppliers, especially heavy ones
Competitors: avoid or cluster
teach.note: Bismillah. Use fictional Greenway Furniture Ltd, planning a factory. Heavy materials (timber) mean being near suppliers cuts transport costs. A restaurant needs footfall. Ask: why do some businesses locate next to competitors? (Customers compare, for example a street of car showrooms.) Ask why a business might avoid competitors.

teach.heading: Nature of the activity
bullets: Retail: busy streets, customers nearby
Manufacturing: space, transport links, cheaper rent
Services: access to clients or work from home
Extraction: where the resource is
teach.note: Link to sector knowledge from last lesson. A fishing business must be near the sea, a call centre can be anywhere with staff and internet, a hairdresser needs customers on foot. Ask pupils to place five fictional businesses (a bakery, a mine, a dentist, a web designer, a warehouse) and justify. Misconception: the cheapest location is not always best; compare cost against revenue.

teach.heading: Worked example: comparing locations
teach.note: Show a simple decision. Pupils should see cost is not the only variable. Ask what other factors might matter (parking, staff travel, competitors). Introduce weighting if time.

model.problem: Greenway Furniture compares two sites. Site A: rent 4,000 pounds a month, transport cost to customers 1,500 pounds. Site B: rent 2,500 pounds a month, transport cost 3,800 pounds. Which is cheaper per month?
model.answer: Site A is 800 pounds a month cheaper

teach.heading: The internet and e-commerce
bullets: Online shops need less high-street space
Can sell nationally or globally from anywhere
Need a warehouse, delivery and a good website
Customers cannot touch or try products
teach.note: Ask: which businesses are hardest to move online? Haircuts, dentists, restaurants. E-commerce means a business can choose a cheap location, but delivery cost and trust matter. Ask pupils to explain why a bakery may still want a shop even though it sells online.

teach.heading: Legal controls and trade blocs
bullets: Planning permission and zoning limit where firms build
Environmental and safety laws affect sites
Trade blocs allow easier trade between members
Firms may locate inside a bloc to avoid tariffs
teach.note: Keep it conceptual. A government may refuse planning permission for a noisy factory near homes. A trade bloc lets members trade with lower tariffs, so a firm outside may build a factory inside to sell freely. Use a fictional bloc: the Blue Sea Trade Union. Ask: how does this help a firm? Cheaper, easier sales. Do not name real bloc membership details.

teach.heading: Check: location
teach.note: Answer D. Heavy bulky materials lead to locating near the source; A and B are not about materials.

check.q: A firm makes cement from heavy limestone and sells to builders nationwide. Which factor is likely most important?
check.why: Heavy, bulky raw materials are expensive to move, so firms tend to locate near them.

practice: A bakery pays rent of 3,200 pounds and delivery costs 900 pounds a month at site A, or rent 2,000 pounds and delivery 2,400 pounds at site B. Which is cheaper and by how much?
State two reasons a hairdresser should locate on a busy street.
Explain how e-commerce changes a business's location choice.
independent: Core: Choose a location for fictional Zam Zam Cafe from three given sites using market, rent and competitors.
Extend: Explain two ways a trade bloc could influence where a clothes manufacturer locates.

Stretch: Justify (6 marks): Should an online toy business rent a warehouse near the capital, where rent is high, or in a smaller town with low rent but poor transport? Use 1,200 orders a week in your reasoning.
exit: Give two location factors.
Define e-commerce.
Big question: for a bakery, one reason for a high-street shop and one for online only.
lessons.homework: Look at three shops near your home and decide which location factor best explains where each is.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a factor checklist with pictures. EAL: pre-teach footfall, proximity. Stretch: weigh factors using a scoring grid and explain the weighting.

lessons.title: Market research: finding out before you spend
lessons.bigQuestion: How can a business find out what customers want without guessing?
objectives: Explain why businesses carry out market research
Describe primary and secondary research methods
Distinguish qualitative from quantitative data and judge reliability
successCriteria: All: define primary and secondary research and name two methods of each
Most: choose a suitable method for a given business and say why
Some: evaluate the reliability of a survey sample
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: sampling, percentages and averages from survey results
lessons.smsc: Moral: honesty and consent when collecting information from people

keywords.def: collecting and analysing information about customers and the market
new information collected first-hand for a specific purpose
existing information collected by someone else
descriptive opinions and feelings
numerical data that can be counted
selling a product in a small area first to gauge reaction
a small group chosen to represent the whole market

starter: Name two location factors.
Define e-commerce.
Why might a business choose a cheaper location even if it is further from customers?

teach.heading: Why research?
bullets: Finds customer needs and gaps in the market
Reduces the risk of failure
Helps set price, product and promotion
Checks reactions to a new idea
teach.note: Bismillah. Use fictional Layla's Lunchbox, a healthy school-meal start-up. She plans to spend 15,000 pounds; asking 200 parents first could save that if nobody wants it. Ask: what could go wrong if she only asks friends? Introduce risk. Ensure pupils see research reduces risk but does not remove it.

teach.heading: Primary research methods
bullets: Surveys and questionnaires
Focus groups: a small group discusses the product
Observation: watching how customers behave
Test marketing: a trial in a small area
teach.note: Match each with Layla's. Questionnaire: 150 parents asked about price. Focus group: eight parents taste samples. Observation: counting how many pupils buy the snacks at the tuck shop. Test marketing: sells at one school for a month. Discuss benefit: relevant and up to date; limitation: expensive and slow.

teach.heading: Secondary research and types of data
teach.note: Compare. Secondary sources: internet, market reports, government reports. Cheaper and fast but may be out of date or not specific. Then link qualitative (a parent says the meals look dull) and quantitative (62 per cent would pay 3 pounds). Ask which data is easier to chart. Note social media can provide both, but opinions on it may not represent all customers.

right.title: Secondary research
points: May be out of date or general

teach.heading: Worked example: reading survey results
teach.note: Model the percentage and the judgement of reliability. Ask whether 40 parents at one school gate is a good sample. Draw out sample size and bias: only one area. Remind pupils that percentages should be calculated from the sample total.

model.problem: Layla surveys 250 parents. 175 say they would buy her lunchbox at 3 pounds. What percentage would buy, and how reliable is it?
steps: Check the sample: 250 parents is reasonably large
But if all came from one school the result may be biased
model.answer: 70% would buy; reliable only if the sample is varied

teach.heading: Check: method
teach.note: Answer C. Question gives a group discussing opinions - focus group. Distractor B is a trial sale.

check.q: Eight parents try Layla's meals and discuss them with a researcher. Which method is this?
check.why: A small group discussing a product with a facilitator is a focus group.

teach.heading: Reliability and social media
bullets: Large, random samples are more reliable
Biased questions give biased answers
Old data may no longer be true
Social media comments are opinions of those who post
teach.note: Ask pupils to spot the bias in 'Don't you agree our delicious meals are great value?' Discuss leading questions. Discuss honesty: Islamic ethics emphasise truthfulness, so a business should report results honestly even if they disappoint. Say that the teacher may expand with class discussion.

practice: Layla's survey: 90 of 120 parents like the idea. Calculate the percentage.
State two advantages of secondary research.
Explain one limitation of a focus group.
independent: Core: Design five questions for a questionnaire for a fictional school uniform shop, including one quantitative and one qualitative.
Extend: Explain why test marketing is useful before a national launch.
Stretch: Evaluate (8 marks): Layla can spend 800 pounds on a survey or use free government reports. Which should she use? Give a judgement.
exit: Define primary research.
Give one qualitative and one quantitative example.
Big question: one way to find out what customers want without guessing.
lessons.homework: Write a short, fair, three-question survey for a business of your choice and ask five people.
lessons.send: SEND: provide sentence starters for survey questions. EAL: use pictures for focus group and observation. Stretch: discuss sample bias with examples.

lessons.title: The market: customers, segments and competition
lessons.bigQuestion: Is it better to sell a little to everybody or a lot to a few?
objectives: Explain what marketing is and why customer relationships matter
Compare market orientation with product orientation and niche with mass marketing
Describe market segmentation by location, demographics, lifestyle, income and age
successCriteria: All: define marketing and name three ways to segment a market
Most: explain niche and mass marketing with an example
Some: judge whether a business should target a niche or mass market
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: market share and percentage change
lessons.smsc: Moral: serving customers' real needs honestly, without exploiting them

keywords.def: identifying and meeting customer needs profitably
a group of customers with similar characteristics
a small, specialised part of a market
a very large market with many customers
designing products around what research says customers want
making a product first, then trying to sell it
customers who keep buying from one business

starter: Name one primary research method.
What is a qualitative result?
Why does a business do market research?

teach.heading: What marketing does
bullets: Identifies customer needs
Meets them with the right product
Builds relationships and loyalty
Responds to changing tastes and spending
teach.note: Bismillah. Use the fictional Tahir's Trainers. Ask: what does marketing mean? Pupils often say adverts; stress it covers research, product, price, place and promotion. Loyalty: a customer who returns costs less than winning a new one. Link to changes: a fall in incomes may mean customers want cheaper shoes, and competition may force a response.

teach.heading: Market orientation and product orientation
teach.note: Show the difference. A market-orientated firm researches first. A product-orientated firm invents then sells. Ask which is riskier. Product orientation can work with a new invention, but only if people want it. Misconception: market orientation does not mean copying competitors; it means responding to customers.

right.title: Product orientation
points: Based on the firm's own idea
Higher risk if nobody wants it

teach.heading: Segmentation
bullets: Location: city, town, region
Demographics: gender, family, occupation
Lifestyle: sporty, quiet, adventurous
Income: budget or luxury
Age: teenagers, adults, over 60s
teach.note: Take Tahir's Trainers and design a plan for each segment. Teenagers who want fashion; over 60s who want comfort; low-income families who need cheap. Ask why segmentation helps: messages, prices and products fit each group. Note the exam may give data by segment and ask which to target.

teach.heading: Niche and mass marketing
teach.note: Table. Niche: small market, higher prices possible, less competition, but limited sales. Mass: many customers, lower prices, economies of scale, but big competitors. Ask which suits a small firm. Ask which would suit a multinational. Evaluate with context.

teach.heading: Worked example: share change
teach.note: Show percentage change as 'change over original'. Note the common error of dividing by the new figure. Then ask whether the firm should be pleased and what else they would want to know (market growth).

model.problem: Tahir's sales rose from 80,000 pounds to 92,000 pounds. The market total stayed at 800,000. Calculate the percentage change in sales and the new market share.

teach.heading: Check: segment
teach.note: Answer B. A is location; C is age; D is income.

check.q: A gym offers evening classes for people who like outdoor sports and healthy eating. Which segmentation is this?
check.why: Interest in outdoor sport and healthy eating describes lifestyle.

practice: Tahir's sales were 50,000 pounds in a market worth 500,000. Calculate market share.
Give three ways to segment the market for a bicycle shop.
Explain one benefit of a niche market.
independent: Core: Segment the market for a fictional cafe by age and income and say what to offer each group.
Extend: Explain why a market-orientated business is less likely to fail.
Stretch: Justify (6 marks): A new bakery with 25,000 pounds of capital can target either the mass market or a niche market for gluten-free cakes. Which should it choose?
exit: Define niche market.
Give two forms of segmentation.
Big question: a little to everyone or a lot to a few? One reason.
lessons.homework: Choose a brand and write which segment it targets and how you know.
lessons.send: SEND: use a segment picture sort. EAL: define demographics with examples. Stretch: link segment choice to price and promotion.

lessons.title: The marketing mix: product, life cycle and the Boston matrix
lessons.bigQuestion: Why do some products last for decades while others vanish within a year?
objectives: Describe the product element of the mix: new product development, goods and services, packaging
Describe the product life cycle and extension strategies
Use the Boston matrix to make portfolio decisions
successCriteria: All: name the four Ps and the stages of the life cycle
Most: describe each Boston matrix category
Some: recommend extension strategies for a product in decline
lessons.crossCurricular: Art and Design: packaging and branding
lessons.smsc: Moral: honest labelling and packaging; avoiding misleading claims

keywords.def: the combination of product, price, place and promotion
the stages a product passes through from launch to decline
action to lengthen a product's life
a tool that classifies products by market share and market growth
high market share in a fast-growing market
high market share in a slow-growing market
low market share in a fast-growing market
low market share in a slow-growing market

starter: Define market segmentation.
Name one niche market.
What is market orientation?

teach.heading: The four Ps and the product
bullets: Product, price, place, promotion
Product: goods or services, design, packaging
New product development: idea, research, testing, launch
Packaging protects, informs and attracts
teach.note: Bismillah. Use fictional Sunrise Juices. Ask pupils to list the four Ps. Then go deep on product: a good must be safe and as described. Packaging must be honest; Islamic ethics value honesty in trade, and the teacher can expand without quoting. New product development: idea, market research, prototype, testing, launch. Many ideas fail: ask why testing saves money.

teach.heading: The product life cycle
teach.note: Use the cycle. Stages: development (cost, no sales), introduction (low sales), growth (rising), maturity (sales peak and level), decline (falling). Ask pupils to place Sunrise's Mango Boost. Extension strategies: new flavours, new packaging, new markets, price cuts, advertising. Misconception: every product reaches decline at a different speed; fashion fast, salt slow.

teach.heading: Extension strategies
bullets: New packaging or design
New flavour or version
Sell in a new market or country
Fresh advertising or a promotion
teach.note: Give Mango Boost, in maturity, sales stuck at 40,000 bottles a month. Ask pupils to choose two strategies and say what each costs. Draw out that extension can reverse falling sales, but costs money and may not work.

teach.heading: Boston matrix
teach.note: Explain axes: market share across, market growth up. Stars need investment, cash cows fund others, problem children could become stars or dogs, dogs may be dropped. Misconception: a dog is not always loss-making, but its prospects are poor. Ask pupils to classify Sunrise's four products with the table.

teach.heading: Check: life cycle
teach.note: Answer A. Sales rising quickly with rising profit is growth. Maturity is level sales.

check.q: Sunrise's Green Detox drink has sales rising fast and new retailers stocking it. Which stage is this?
check.why: Quickly rising sales as more retailers stock the product is the growth stage.

teach.heading: Worked example: using the matrix
teach.note: Model a decision from numbers. Ask: what would you do with a dog? Answer options: drop, or reposition. Remind that the matrix is a snapshot and needs updating.

model.problem: Sunrise's Plain Apple has 3% market share in a market growing 1% a year, and costs 12,000 pounds to make. What should the firm consider?
steps: Low share and low growth: this is a dog
Option: stop selling and use the money elsewhere
Option: check whether it helps the sales of other products before dropping
model.answer: Likely to drop it, unless it supports other sales

practice: Place a product with falling sales and fewer shops stocking it in the life cycle.
Give two extension strategies for a snack in maturity.
Explain what a business should do with a star product.
independent: Core: Draw a life cycle graph and label each stage for a fictional phone.
Extend: Explain how packaging can add value to a product.
Stretch: Evaluate (8 marks): A firm with one cash cow, two stars and two dogs has 100,000 pounds to invest. How should it allocate it?
exit: Name the stages of the life cycle.
What is a cash cow?
Big question: one reason products last for decades.
lessons.homework: Choose a product you know and place it on the life cycle and the Boston matrix with reasons.
lessons.send: SEND: give a labelled life-cycle diagram. EAL: use images for star, cash cow, dog. Stretch: investigate how extension strategies changed a real product.

lessons.title: The marketing mix: pricing strategies
lessons.bigQuestion: How low can you price a product before it stops paying?
objectives: Describe cost-plus, penetration, competition, skimming and promotional pricing
Calculate a cost-plus price
Choose a pricing strategy for a given situation
successCriteria: All: name five pricing strategies
Most: calculate a cost-plus selling price
Some: justify a pricing strategy using evidence
lessons.smsc: Moral: fair pricing and avoiding unfair profiteering; the teacher may draw on class discussion of fairness in trade

keywords.def: adding a fixed percentage or amount to unit cost
a low launch price to win customers
a high launch price for a new, desirable product
setting price in line with rivals
temporary price cuts such as sales and offers
the cost of making one item

starter: Name the four Ps.
What is a niche market?
Name the five stages of the life cycle.

teach.heading: Why price matters
bullets: Price affects sales, profit and image
Too high loses customers
Too low may not cover costs
Must fit target customers
teach.note: Bismillah. Use fictional Zahra's Bags. If the bag costs 18 pounds to make and sells for 15, the business loses. Ask pupils what else price signals: quality. Fairness: a business that raises prices unfairly because customers have no other choice can damage trust; teachers can expand on ethics in trade without quoting.

teach.heading: Five strategies
bullets: Cost-plus: unit cost plus a markup
Penetration: low price to enter the market
Skimming: high price for a new, exciting product
Competitive: match rivals' prices
Promotional: short-term offers
teach.note: Give each a quick scenario. Zahra's: cost-plus to ensure profit. A new smartwatch uses skimming to earn from early adopters. A cafe next to rivals uses competitive pricing. A launch sale uses promotional pricing. Penetration requires being able to bear lower profit early; risk of customers leaving when price rises.

teach.heading: Worked example: cost-plus
teach.note: Ask pupils to add markup to cost. Check that 40 per cent markup is of cost, not of selling price. Extend: profit per bag = 7.20; for 500 bags sold profit 3,600.

model.problem: A bag costs 18 pounds to make. Zahra adds a 40% markup. Find the selling price, and the profit on 500 bags.

teach.heading: Choosing a strategy
teach.note: Use table to link strategy to situation. Pupils practise matching. Drive the point that the best strategy depends on the market, product and aims. Skimming is risky if copied quickly.

head: Strategy
Best when
Risk
rows: Low profit, hard to raise price

teach.heading: Check: strategy
