teach.note: Answer B. Setting a low launch price to win customers quickly is penetration.

check.q: A new streaming app sets a very low price in its first three months to gain subscribers. Which strategy is this?
check.why: A low price to enter a market and win customers fast is penetration pricing. Promotional pricing is also temporary, but its aim is short-term sales on established products.

teach.heading: Evaluating price decisions
bullets: Look at costs, competitors and customers
Consider the product's life cycle stage
Think about the image the price creates
Judge short-term versus long-term effect
teach.note: Tell pupils that in evaluation questions, they should weigh up at least two factors and make a decision. Give an example: Zahra's has 30 rivals selling at 22 pounds. Cost-plus at 25.20 might lose customers; competitive pricing may reduce profit but keep sales.

practice: A cake costs 6 pounds. Add a 50% markup. What is the price?
Explain one risk of penetration pricing.
State two reasons a business might use promotional pricing.
independent: Core: Calculate cost-plus prices for five items with different markups.
Extend: Explain why price skimming suits a new gadget but not a loaf of bread.
Stretch: Justify (6 marks): Zahra's Bags can use cost-plus at 25.20 pounds or match rivals at 22 pounds. Which, and why? Use unit cost 18 pounds.
exit: Define price skimming.
Calculate selling price with cost 40 pounds and markup 25%.
Big question: how low before it stops paying?
lessons.homework: Compare the prices of one product at three shops and say which strategy each seems to use.
lessons.send: SEND: give a markup calculation template. EAL: define penetration and skimming with images. Stretch: link pricing strategies to the product life cycle.

lessons.title: The marketing mix: place and promotion
lessons.bigQuestion: Does a good product sell itself?
objectives: Describe retailers and e-tailers as places to sell
Describe advertising, sponsorship, trials, offers, branding and public relations
Distinguish above-the-line from below-the-line promotion and explain online promotion
successCriteria: All: name two routes to market and four promotion methods
Most: classify promotion as above or below the line
Some: justify a promotion mix for a given business
lessons.crossCurricular: English: persuasive and advertising language; Computer Science: e-commerce
lessons.smsc: Moral: truthful advertising; avoiding misleading or manipulative claims

keywords.def: a business that sells goods to the public from shops
a retailer that sells online
creating a name and identity that customers recognise
promotion in media for a mass audience, such as TV and press
direct promotion, such as offers and trials
managing the image a business has with the public
content shared quickly between users on social media

starter: Define penetration pricing.
Calculate cost 20 pounds plus markup 30%.
Name a stage of the product life cycle.

teach.heading: Place: how goods reach customers
bullets: Retailers: shops, supermarkets, markets
E-tailers: websites and apps
Direct from producer to customer
Choice depends on product and customers
teach.note: Bismillah. Use fictional Noor's Notebooks. Compare shop: customers can see the product, immediate sale, high rent. Online: wider reach, lower rent, delivery cost, returns. Ask: which suits a product that must be tried on? Shop. Link to location lesson on e-commerce.

teach.heading: Promotion methods
bullets: Advertising: TV, radio, press, posters
Sponsorship: paying to be linked with an event
Trials: free samples to try
Offers: discounts, buy one get one free
Branding and PR: build image and trust
teach.note: Ask for an example of each from pupils' lives. Add honesty: adverts must not lie; misleading claims can break the law and the trust of customers. Ask which methods cost most. TV is expensive for a small firm; a free sample may suit a local business.

teach.heading: Above and below the line
teach.note: Table. Teachers: stress above the line is mass media and below the line is direct to customers. Common error: sponsorship is often placed above the line; accept with explanation. PR sits in its own category in many courses; treat it as separate if the class prefers.

head: Type
Meaning
Examples
Cost and reach
rows: Mass media for a wide audience
Free samples, discount vouchers, direct mail

teach.heading: Online promotion
bullets: Targeted adverts based on interests
Viral social media posts shared by users
E-newsletters to subscribers
Cheaper and measurable, but needs managing
teach.note: Show how targeted adverts can reach only 15 to 18 year olds, reducing waste. Viral: one funny video shared by 20,000 users. E-newsletters: low cost, only reach people who signed up. Risks: negative comments spread as quickly. Ask pupils to suggest a viral idea for Noor's Notebooks and then discuss honesty and respect in content.

teach.heading: Worked example: promotion cost per sale
teach.note: Model cost-effectiveness. Ask which is better value and what else to consider (reach and long-term brand).

model.problem: Noor's Notebooks spends 600 pounds on a radio advert and gains 150 sales. It spends 240 pounds on targeted online adverts and gains 120 sales. Which cost less per sale?
steps: Online is half the cost per sale
model.answer: Online adverts: 2 pounds per sale against 4 pounds

teach.heading: Check: classify
teach.note: Answer C. Free samples are direct promotion to customers: below the line.

check.q: A juice company hands out free samples outside a school. Which type of promotion is this?
check.why: Free samples are a trial and are below the line. TV or national press would be above the line.

practice: Noor's spends 900 pounds on an advert that gains 300 sales. Calculate the cost per sale.
State two benefits of selling through an e-tailer.
Explain why a small business might use below-the-line promotion.
independent: Core: Match ten promotion examples to above or below the line.
Extend: Explain two risks of viral social media marketing.
Stretch: Evaluate (8 marks): With 2,000 pounds, should a new local cafe use a radio advert or social media and free samples? Give a reasoned judgement.
exit: Define branding.
Give one difference between a retailer and an e-tailer.
Big question: does a good product sell itself? One reason it needs promotion.
lessons.homework: Collect two adverts you see this week and classify the type of promotion.
lessons.send: SEND: use a sorting card set. EAL: show brand logos for branding. Stretch: design a promotion mix for 500 pounds.

lessons.title: Communication in business: methods, barriers and IT
lessons.bigQuestion: Why can one unclear message cost a business thousands?
objectives: Explain why good communication matters
Describe communication methods, including IT, with benefits and limitations
Identify barriers to communication and ways to remove them
successCriteria: All: name three communication methods and two barriers
Most: explain benefits and limitations of email and meetings
Some: choose and justify a method for a given message
lessons.crossCurricular: English: formal and informal writing; Computer Science: digital communication
lessons.smsc: Moral: truthful, respectful communication (adab) with colleagues and customers

keywords.def: passing information from a sender to a receiver and getting feedback
the method used to send a message
anything that stops a message being understood
the receiver's response confirming the message was understood
specialist words that others may not understand

starter: Define above the line promotion.
Give one benefit of an e-tailer.
State one promotion method.

teach.heading: Why communication matters
bullets: Staff know what to do and when
Fewer mistakes and wasted costs
Customers get accurate information
Better teamwork and morale
teach.note: Bismillah. Use fictional Lantern Logistics: a manager emails 'deliver the order tomorrow' but not which address, and 3,000 pounds of goods go to the wrong place. Ask pupils to calculate the cost of a mistake. Then link to adab: polite, clear, truthful speech in the workplace.

teach.heading: Methods and IT
teach.note: Table. Stress the exam wants benefits and limitations in context. Choose the channel to fit the message: urgent, private, formal, many people. Ask pupils which method for dismissal (face to face, with a letter), a team update (email), an urgent change (phone or messaging app).

head: Method
Benefit
Limitation
rows: Face to face from far away

teach.heading: Barriers to communication
bullets: Jargon and unclear language
Too many layers of management
Language or cultural differences
Technology failure or information overload
Poor listening or no feedback
teach.note: Ask pupils for an example of each in Lantern Logistics. Discuss how much more difficult communication becomes in a large business with sites in many countries and time zones. Ask for solutions: simple language, fewer layers, translation, backup systems, checking understanding.

teach.heading: Removing barriers
bullets: Use plain language and short messages
Check understanding with feedback
Train staff to listen
Use the right channel for the message
teach.note: Make the solution part of each barrier. Misconception: IT removes all barriers; it can create new ones, such as too many emails. Ask: how do you check understanding? Ask the receiver to repeat the task in their own words.

teach.heading: Worked example: choosing a channel
teach.note: Model the reasoning. Ask pupils to give a different choice and justify it. The point is that justification, not the answer, earns marks.

model.problem: Lantern Logistics must tell 40 drivers that a road is closed from 6am tomorrow. Choose a channel and justify.
steps: A group messaging app reaches everyone quickly
Limitation: some may not read it, so ask for a reply to confirm
model.answer: Group messaging app with confirmation replies

teach.heading: Check: barrier
teach.note: Answer A. Jargon is a language barrier. B and C are solutions, not barriers.

check.q: A manager fills an instruction with technical abbreviations the new staff do not know. What is this barrier?
check.why: Specialist words the receiver does not know are jargon, a common barrier.

practice: Give one benefit and one limitation of email.
Lantern's mistake cost 3,000 pounds on each of 4 wrong deliveries. Calculate the total cost.
Suggest two ways to remove a language barrier.
independent: Core: Match six messages to the best channel and explain each.
Extend: Explain two ways IT has changed communication for a business with sites in three countries.
Stretch: Analyse (6 marks): A manager communicates only by email with a team of fifteen. Analyse two problems and recommend improvements.
exit: Define barrier to communication.
Name one communication method and one limitation.
Big question: how can one unclear message cost thousands? Answer in a sentence.
lessons.homework: Rewrite a confusing instruction in plain language and say which barrier you removed.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a sentence frame for choosing a channel. EAL: pre-teach jargon with examples. Stretch: discuss communication in large multinational teams.

lessons.title: Recruitment and selection: finding the right person
lessons.bigQuestion: What makes the right person for the job?
objectives: Describe types of employment and recruitment documents
Compare internal and external recruitment and describe the process
Explain legal controls: equal opportunities and minimum wage
successCriteria: All: define job description and person specification and name three employment types
Most: compare internal and external recruitment
Some: justify a recruitment method and explain legal controls
lessons.crossCurricular: English: CV and application writing; PSHE: careers
lessons.smsc: Moral: justice and equal treatment in hiring; fair pay and honest dealing

keywords.def: a document listing the duties of a job
the skills, qualities and experience needed in the post holder
narrowing applicants to those who best match the specification
filling a post from existing staff
filling a post from outside the business
the lowest hourly pay the law allows
laws and policies preventing unfair discrimination at work

starter: Name two communication barriers.
Give one benefit of face to face communication.
Define jargon.

teach.heading: Types of employment
bullets: Full-time and part-time
Job share: two people share one job
Casual, temporary and seasonal
Choice depends on demand and cost
teach.note: Bismillah. Use fictional Seaside Ice Cream, busy in summer only. Ask which type fits. Seasonal staff in summer; casual cover for busy weekends; a full-time manager all year. Benefits to the firm: flexibility, lower cost. Drawbacks: less commitment, need to train again each year.

teach.heading: Recruitment documents
bullets: Job description: duties and conditions
Person specification: skills and qualities needed
Application form or CV from applicants
References from past employers
teach.note: Show a short job description and person specification for a shop assistant. Pupils decide which statement belongs in each. Misconception: the two are often confused: one describes the job, the other describes the person.

teach.heading: The process
teach.note: Use cycle. At shortlisting, the firm compares each application to the person specification. At interview it asks questions and may add tests. Honesty: applicants should be honest on CVs, and employers honest about the job, which links to trust and truthfulness in dealing.
cycle: Write job description and person specification

teach.heading: Internal and external recruitment
teach.note: Compare. Internal: cheaper, quicker, motivates staff, who know the firm, but a smaller choice and creates a gap elsewhere. External: new ideas and bigger choice, but costly and slower, and new staff need induction. Ask pupils which they would choose for a manager role.

teach.heading: Legal controls
bullets: Equal opportunities: no unfair discrimination
Minimum wage: lowest legal hourly rate
Firms must follow the law in every country they operate in
Breaking the law risks fines and a poor reputation
teach.note: Keep it factual: do not quote specific current wage figures unless given in a question. Use fictional numbers. Equal opportunities: choose by skills, not by unrelated personal characteristics. Fair treatment of workers is also a theme in Islamic ethics; the teacher may expand and invite pupils to discuss.

teach.heading: Check: document
teach.note: Answer B. The person specification describes the person; the job description describes the duties.

check.q: Which document lists the skills and qualities a successful applicant should have?
check.why: The person specification describes the ideal person. The job description lists duties; confusing the two is the usual error.

teach.heading: Worked example: cost of a recruitment
teach.note: Model the calculation and then the evaluation: cheaper does not always mean better. Ask what else matters: skills and fit with the specification.

model.problem: Seaside Ice Cream pays 450 pounds to advertise a post externally. Internal recruitment would cost 100 pounds of manager time. The new employee will be paid 9 pounds an hour for 30 hours a week. Find the extra cost of external recruitment and the weekly wage.
steps: Compare: the extra cost equals more than one week's wage
model.answer: 350 pounds extra; wage 270 pounds a week

practice: Seaside needs 6 seasonal staff for 12 weeks at 8 pounds an hour for 20 hours a week. Calculate the total wage bill.
State one benefit and one drawback of internal recruitment.
Explain why a person specification helps with shortlisting.
independent: Core: Write a job description and a person specification for a fictional shop assistant.
Extend: Explain two reasons why Seaside Ice Cream might use seasonal staff.

Stretch: Justify (6 marks): A cafe needs a new manager. Should it promote its supervisor or recruit externally? Use the information that the supervisor has two years' experience and the cafe needs new ideas.
exit: Define equal opportunities.
Name two types of employment.
Big question: what makes the right person for the job?
lessons.homework: Find a real job advert and identify one duty and one skill required.
lessons.send: SEND: provide labelled examples of job description and person specification. EAL: pre-teach vacancy, shortlist. Stretch: investigate why job sharing might help some workers.
